name: Mushuau Innu / Davis Inlet Naskapi
confidence_why: one confirmed first-hand source; 12 other works read were silent
catalog_citation: Scott, Mark Andrew. 2000. Phonological sketch of Mushuau Innu (Davis Inlet Naskapi). MA thesis, Memorial University of Newfoundland. xx+251 pp. (MUN Scholaris hdl 20.500.14783/12891; mirror innu-aimun.ca)
catalog_locator: sec. 3.2 'Accent', thesis pp. 190-191 (PDF pp. 207-208) and p. 203 (PDF p. 220); evidence pp. 191-203; restated ch. 4 pp. 242-243 (PDF pp. 259-260). Saved file: the copy we hold; page renders the copy we hold
catalog_quote: [pp. 190-191] Mushuau Innu has iambic feet (for a discussion of metrical theory see section 1.9.6.); word accent occurs on the head of the rightmost iambic foot. The direction of parsing is left to right. Final syllables are optionally extrametrical. Stray light syllables are not parsed into feet. This accentual system is different from that of many Montagnais dialects which have accent on word-final syllables ... The Mushuau Innu accentual system does not recognize coda material as contributing to syllable weight ...; therefore syllable weight is determined by vowel length alone: a long vowel forms the nucleus of a heavy syllable and a short vowel forms the nucleus of a light syllable. [p. 203] In conclusion, accent must fall within the last three syllables of a Mushuau Innu word. This is achieved through right to left parsing of syllables into iambic feet and accentuation of the head of the rightmost foot in the word, along with optional final-syllable extrametricality (as well, stray light syllables are not parsed into feet). Syllable weight is determined by vowel length alone, with the exception of word-final /mʷ/ which contributes to syllable weight. There is an accent retraction process which draws the accent of a word to the left edge of the accentual domain when the word is preceded by another word in the phonological phrase.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive right-edge iambic system: syllables with long vowels are heavy (codas do not count, except word-final /mʷ/); build iambs (L H, L L, or lone H) and stress the head of the rightmost foot, so primary accent normally lands on the last long vowel within a final three-syllable window -- final if the last syllable is heavy and not extrametrical, penult when the final syllable is (optionally) extrametrical or a stray light syllable, antepenult when both the final is extrametrical and the penult is a stray light syllable; never further left than the antepenult.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Author reports hearing secondary stress on some words in the recordings (taken as evidence for multiple feet) but relies on Mailhot's transcription of primary stress only and does not analyse secondary stress (p. 193 fn. 121).
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final light syllables closed by /mʷ/ can bear accent (e.g. wa:pa:'tum 'he sees'); considerable token-to-token variation (ta:'ha:w ~ 'ta:ha:w) attributed to optional final extrametricality; an 'accent retraction' drawing accent to the left edge of the three-syllable window when the word is preceded by another word in the phonological phrase; two residual unexplained items (760-761, p. 202-203). Note the thesis says 'left to right' parsing on p.191 but 'right to left' on p.198 and in both conclusions (pp. 203, 242).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent from José Mailhot's 1971 elicited single-word citation forms (Davis Inlet); phrase-level retraction noted but not studied. Explicitly contrasted with the consistent word-final accent of most Montagnais (Innu) dialects.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Mushuau Innu = Davis Inlet (now Natuashish, Labrador) 'Eastern Naskapi', based on Mailhot's 1971 recordings; Glottolog 5.1 files Scott 2000 under nask1242 and ISO nsk covers both Eastern and Western Naskapi, but the community usually meant by 'Naskapi' today is Western Naskapi at Kawawachikamach (ex Fort Chimo), for which no first-hand stress rule was located. MacKenzie 1980 (pp. 45-49, Map 2-4, R6b p. 250-251) groups both Naskapi varieties with the northern palatalized y-dialects having NON-final stress ('not well understood'; 'usually the rightmost underlying long vowel'), and flags Fort Chimo as behaving differently in one derivation, so the Davis Inlet rule should not be assumed to transfer unchanged to Kawawachikamach.

sources.note: Sec. 2.2 'Stress Placement' pp. 45-49 with Map 2-4: two patterns in the palatalized dialects, word-final (n/l Montagnais, area of French influence) vs non-final (y-dialects incl. the northern ones); for non-final dialects 'it is difficult to formulate a rule.. stress usually falls on the rightmost underlying long vowel'; stress shift marks inanimate plural after apocope; appendix R6b p.250-251: 'The assignment of primary stress is not well understood for the palatalized-y dialects', with Fort Chimo (FC = Western Naskapi) flagged as an exception in Ex18. CMN-wide, no Naskapi-specific rule.
